ety.text: Anglo-Norman suitebor. Middle English sute English suit Inherited from Middle English sute, borrowed from Anglo-Norman suite, from metathesis of earlier Old French siute, from Vulgar Latin *sequita, from *sequere, from sequor, sequi, from Proto-Italic *sekʷōr, from Proto-Indo-European *sékʷetor, from *sekʷ-. Doublet of suite. Cognate with Italian seguire and Spanish seguir. Related to sue and segue.

senses.d: A set of clothes to be worn together, now especially a man's matching jacket and trousers (also business suit or lounge suit), or a similar outfit for a woman.
ex: Nick hired a navy-blue suit for the wedding.

senses.d: A garment or set of garments suitable and/or required for a given task or activity: space suit, boiler suit, protective suit, swimsuit.
A dress.
A person who wears matching jacket and trousers, especially a boss or a supervisor.
ex: Be sure to keep your nose to the grindstone today; the suits are making a "surprise" visit to this department.
You had an army / Of suits behind you

senses.d: A full set of armour.
The attempt to gain an end by legal process; a process instituted in a court of law for the recovery of a right or claim; a lawsuit.
ex: If you take my advice, you'll file a suit against him immediately.

senses.d: Petition, request, entreaty.
The act of following or pursuing; pursuit, chase.
Pursuit of a love-interest; wooing, courtship.
ex:
Rebate your loves, each rival suit suspend,

senses.d: The act of suing; the pursuit of a particular object or goal.
ex: Thenceforth the suitt of earthly conquest shonne.

senses.d: To make proper or suitable; to adapt or fit.

senses.d: To be suitable or apt for one's image.

senses.d: To be appropriate or apt for.
ex: The nickname "Bullet" suits her, since she is a fast runner.

senses.d: To dress; to clothe.

senses.d: To please; to make content; to fit someone's (or one's own) taste.
ex: will build to suit   [on for-sale signs marking vacant lots]
He is well suited with his place.

senses.d: To agree; to be fitted; to correspond (usually followed by to, archaically also followed by with).
ex: The place itself was suiting to his care.
Give me not an office / That suits with me so ill.

First attested in Thomas Browne's Religio Medici (1643) in noun sense 1, ostensibly from New Latin suīcīdium, from suī (genitive reflexive pronoun) + -cīdium (“act of killing or murder”), but often believed to have originated in English before entering Latin. Displaced native Middle English seolf-cwale from Old English selfcwalu (literally “self-slaughter”), after which suicide may have been modelled, or calqued (compare manuscript).

senses.d: The act of intentionally killing oneself.
ex: As a nation of freemen, we must live through all time, or die by suicide.
The cowardice of suicide was abhorrent to him.

senses.d: A particular instance of a person intentionally killing oneself, or of multiple people doing so.
ex: There had been half a dozen mysterious suicides which had been investigated by Scotland Yard.

senses.d: A person who has intentionally killed themself.
ex: "I remember one suicide," she said to Philip, "who threw himself into the Thames."

senses.d: An action that could cause the literal or figurative death of a person or organization, although death may not be the aim of the action.
ex: political suicide
[…] I do not want the Congress or the country to commit fiscal suicide on the installment plan.

senses.d: A beverage combining all available flavors at a soda fountain.
ex: Using Coca-Cola as a base, a suicide called for the addition of every other flavor available.

senses.d: A diabolo trick where one of the sticks is released and allowed to rotate 360° round the diabolo until it is caught by the hand that released it.
A run comprising a series of sprints of increasing lengths, each followed immediately by a return to the start, with no pause between one sprint and the next.
ex: The coach makes us run suicides at the end of each basketball practice.

senses.d: A children's game of throwing a ball against a wall and at other players, who are eliminated by being struck.
Pertaining to a suicide bombing.
ex: suicide belt
suicide vest

senses.d: To intentionally kill oneself.
ex: "Her husband suicided three years ago. Just like a man!"
Seems a lady poet suicided at Verringer's ranch in Sepulveda canyon one time.

senses.d: To kill (someone) and make their death appear to have been a suicide rather than a homicide (now especially as part of a conspiracy).
ex: Even if he did get charged, he would be suicided long before he could involve one of the city's most important politicians in the scam.

senses.d: To destroy or self-destruct.
